BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) -- A former Colombian congressman who was held hostage in the jungle for more than eight years has escaped -- with the help of a former captor. Oscar Tulio Lizcano was kidnapped on August 4, 2000 near the Colombian town of Riosucio. Oscar Tulio Lizcano, his hair disheveled, appeared too weak to stand for long when he met the news media Sunday, hours after stumbling onto a military patrol -- and freedom. Lizcano suffered from hunger and disease in captivity and endured isolation in the company of leftist rebels who often would not let him talk, he and Colombian authorities said. "Maybe my incoherence is for a lack of speaking," Lizcano told reporters. "I was unable to talk with the guerillas who guarded me." Lizcano said he had little to read in the jungle except "The Odyssey" by Homer. He suffered from malaria and other illnesses and once ate nothing but hearts of palm for six or seven days, said Juan Manuel Santos, the Colombian defense minister. "This is big news for the whole family," said Lizcano's sister, Amparo Lizcano. "We were waiting for the guerrillas to give our brother back alive before he died." The former congressman fled about three days ago with the assistance of one of his captors, a member of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, a leftist rebel force that has been fighting the government for more than 40 years in a war that also has involved right-wing paramilitaries and drug traffickers.  Watch release of FARC hostage » . President Alvaro Uribe appeared on television Sunday with the ex-FARC rebel -- known by the alias "Isaza" -- and said the man will receive compensation and permission to resettle in France with his family. He said that's in keeping with a Colombian government policy that rewards rebels who desert and help hostages gain their freedom. Police officers and soldiers pinpointed the location of the FARC unit holding Lizcano several months ago, Santos said. They monitored the location for about five months and took steps to seal off possible escape routes, he said, as they planned a rescue operation using information gleaned help from a rebel who deserted October 2. Troops started that rescue operation Saturday -- only to discover that "Isaza" and Lizcano had decided on their own to escape. The two men wandered through the jungle for three days and nights before encountering a Colombian army patrol Sunday, said Santos, the defense minister. Lizcano was kidnapped on August 4, 2000 near the Colombian town of Riosucio. He and his former captor stumbled Sunday onto a patrol near the border of the states of Risaralda and Choco, in central Colombia, authorities said. The FARC holds an estimated 750 hostages in Colombia. Its members have justified hostage taking as a legitimate military tactic. The rebels have been battered this year by government raids that killed several top commanders, the death by apparent heart attack of their founder and a wave of desertions. Government commandoes tricked the FARC in July and freed their most prized hostage, the former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, in an elaborate ruse that also liberated three U.S. defense contractors and 11 other hostages. On Sunday, Lizcano offered words of encouragement to those hundreds who remain trapped in the jungle, captives of the FARC. "Hold on. Hold on," he said. "One day you will enjoy your freedom, too." -- CNN's Karl Penhaul contributed to this report .

He endured hunger and illness throughout his captivity, along with prolonged isolation at the hands of leftist rebels who frequently forbade him from speaking, according to both Lizcano and Colombian authorities.

"Perhaps my incoherence stems from a lack of speaking," Lizcano told reporters. "I was unable to converse with the guerrillas who guarded me."

Lizcano recounted having little to read in the jungle beyond a copy of Homer's "The Odyssey." He suffered from malaria and other ailments, and on one occasion subsisted for six or seven days on nothing but hearts of palm, according to Colombian Defense Minister Juan Manuel Santos.

"This is momentous news for the entire family," said Lizcano's sister, Amparo Lizcano. "We had been waiting for the guerrillas to return our brother to us alive, before it was too late."

The former congressman fled approximately three days ago with the help of one of his captors—a member of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, the leftist rebel group that has waged war against the government for more than four decades in a conflict that has also drawn in right-wing paramilitaries and drug traffickers.

Watch release of FARC hostage »

President Álvaro Uribe appeared on television Sunday alongside the former FARC rebel—known by the alias "Isaza"—announcing that the man would receive financial compensation and permission to resettle with his family in France. Uribe explained that this arrangement reflects the Colombian government's policy of rewarding rebels who defect and assist hostages in securing their freedom.

According to Santos, police and military forces had pinpointed the location of the FARC unit holding Lizcano several months earlier. They monitored the area for roughly five months, taking measures to seal off potential escape routes as they devised a rescue operation—one informed by intelligence provided by a rebel who had deserted on October 2. Troops launched that operation on Saturday, only to discover that "Isaza" and Lizcano had already resolved to escape on their own. The two men wandered through the jungle for three days and nights before encountering a Colombian army patrol on Sunday, Santos said.

Lizcano and his former captor emerged from the jungle Sunday near the border of the Risaralda and Chocó departments in central Colombia, authorities reported.

On Sunday, Lizcano offered words of hope to the hundreds still held captive in the jungle by the FARC. "Hold on. Hold on," he urged. "One day, you too will know freedom."

# Colombian Ex-Lawmaker Breaks Free After Eight Years in Captivity, Aided by Guard

BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) — After being held captive in the jungle for over eight years, a former Colombian congressman managed to break free with assistance from one of his own guards. Oscar Tulio Lizcano had been abducted on August 4, 2000, close to the town of Riosucio in Colombia.

When Lizcano faced reporters on Sunday—just hours after encountering a military patrol and gaining his freedom—his tousled hair and evident frailty made it clear he could barely remain standing. Both Lizcano and Colombian officials described the ordeal he endured: illness, hunger, and prolonged isolation among leftist guerrillas who frequently prohibited him from speaking.

"My difficulty forming words might come from being unable to talk for so long," Lizcano explained to journalists. "The guerrillas guarding me wouldn't let me communicate."

According to Lizcano, his only reading material during captivity had been Homer's "The Odyssey." Defense Minister Juan Manuel Santos noted that Lizcano battled malaria along with other ailments, and at one stretch survived on nothing but palm hearts for nearly a week.

"The whole family is overjoyed by this news," Lizcano's sister Amparo shared. "We'd been hoping the guerrillas would return our brother to us alive, before it was too late."

Roughly three days before his reappearance, the former congressman had fled captivity with help from a rebel fighter belonging to the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC)—the leftist guerrilla group that has waged war against the government for four decades, in a conflict that has also drawn in right-wing paramilitary groups and narcotics traffickers.

President Alvaro Uribe made a joint television appearance Sunday alongside the defector, identified only by his alias "Isaza." Uribe announced the former rebel would receive financial compensation and the chance to relocate to France with his family—consistent with government policy that offers incentives to guerrillas who abandon FARC and assist hostages in escaping.

Santos revealed that security forces had identified the whereabouts of the FARC unit holding Lizcano months earlier. Over roughly five months, they kept watch on the location and worked to block potential escape paths, developing a rescue plan using intelligence provided by a rebel who had defected on October 2. Although troops launched their rescue mission on Saturday, they found that Lizcano and "Isaza" had already taken matters into their own hands. The pair spent three days and nights navigating the jungle before crossing paths with an army patrol on Sunday near where the Risaralda and Choco states meet in central Colombia.

FARC is estimated to be holding around 750 hostages throughout Colombia, defending the practice as a valid strategy of warfare. The group has faced significant setbacks this year—government operations eliminated multiple senior commanders, its founder reportedly died of a heart attack, and numerous fighters have defected.

In July, a government operation outwitted FARC through an elaborate deception, securing the release of Ingrid Betancourt—their most valuable hostage and a former presidential candidate—along with three American defense contractors and eleven additional captives.

Before concluding his remarks Sunday, Lizcano directed a message of hope toward the hundreds still held captive by FARC in the jungle: "Keep holding on. Keep holding on. Your day of freedom will come too."

*— CNN's Karl Penhaul contributed to this report.*

# Former Colombian Congressman Escapes FARC Captivity After Eight-Year Ordeal

Oscar Tulio Lizcano, a former Colombian congressman, has finally regained his freedom after enduring more than eight years as a hostage of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) in the country's dense jungle terrain. Lizcano was originally abducted on August 4, 2000, beginning an ordeal that would keep him isolated from his family and the outside world for over eight years.

## An Escape Aided by an Unlikely Ally

What makes Lizcano's escape particularly notable is the role played by one of his own captors in securing his freedom. A FARC rebel known by the alias "Isaza" made the decision to defect from the guerrilla organization and assist Lizcano in fleeing captivity. The pair reportedly spent approximately three days on the run together through the jungle before finally being discovered and reaching safety. This act of defection highlights the internal fractures that have periodically emerged within FARC's ranks, particularly as the Colombian government has intensified efforts to encourage rebels to abandon the insurgency.

## The Toll of Prolonged Captivity

During his more than eight years in the jungle, Lizcano faced brutal physical and psychological hardships. He contracted malaria at some point during his captivity, a serious illness that can be particularly dangerous without adequate medical care in remote jungle conditions. Beyond the disease, Lizcano endured prolonged periods of isolation, cut off from any meaningful human contact beyond his captors. Perhaps most strikingly, he described extended stretches—sometimes lasting six or seven consecutive days—during which his only sustenance was hearts of palm, a stark illustration of the deprivation hostages held by FARC frequently experienced in Colombia's remote jungle camps.

## Government Response and Incentives for Defection

Following news of the successful escape, Colombian President Alvaro Uribe publicly announced that "Isaza," the defecting rebel who helped facilitate Lizcano's freedom, would receive financial compensation for his actions. Additionally, the government pledged to grant him permission to resettle in France, offering him a fresh start far removed from the conflict in Colombia. This response is consistent with a broader government policy designed to incentivize FARC members to assist hostages in gaining their freedom, offering defectors both material rewards and safe passage as a means of encouraging further defections and weakening the guerrilla organization from within.

## Months of Surveillance Preceded the Breakthrough

The successful escape did not occur in isolation but was the culmination of extensive intelligence-gathering efforts by Colombian security forces. Police and military units had been tracking the specific location of the FARC unit holding Lizcano for several months leading up to his escape. This sustained surveillance effort likely played a crucial role in creating the conditions that ultimately allowed for Lizcano's rescue, demonstrating the Colombian government's ongoing commitment to locating and freeing hostages held by the FARC, even in cases where captivity has extended for many years.

Lizcano, who was abducted by FARC guerrillas in 2000 while serving as a member of Colombia's Congress, endured years of grueling conditions deep in the Colombian jungle. Like many hostages held by the leftist rebel group, he suffered from tropical diseases, malnutrition, and the psychological toll of prolonged isolation from his family and the outside world. The FARC, which has used hostage-taking as both a political weapon and a source of leverage in negotiations with the government, held Lizcano among dozens of other captives, including politicians, soldiers, and police officers, in remote camps scattered throughout the country's dense forests.

The breakthrough in Lizcano's captivity came when Isaza, one of the rebels assigned to guard him, agreed to help him flee. According to accounts of the escape, the guard grew disillusioned with the FARC's cause and decided to assist his prisoner rather than continue serving as his jailer. Together, the two men made their way out of guerrilla-controlled territory, eventually reaching safety and ending Lizcano's ordeal after more than eight grueling years in captivity.

Colombian authorities hailed the escape as a significant victory not only for Lizcano and his family, who had campaigned tirelessly for his release, but also for the government's broader strategy of encouraging rebels to defect from FARC's ranks. For years, Colombian President Álvaro Uribe's administration had implemented a policy of offering incentives — including financial rewards, legal amnesty, and resettlement assistance — to guerrilla fighters willing to abandon the insurgency and help secure the release of hostages.

In recognition of his role in facilitating Lizcano's freedom, the Colombian government rewarded Isaza with a cash payment and arranged for his resettlement in France, effectively granting him a new life far removed from the conflict that had defined his years as a FARC fighter. The move was seen as part of a broader effort by Bogotá to weaken the FARC from within by demonstrating to rank-and-file guerrillas that defection could lead to tangible benefits and a path toward reintegration into civilian life.

The FARC, founded in 1964 as a Marxist guerrilla movement, has been engaged in a decades-long armed conflict with the Colombian state, financing its operations partly through kidnappings, extortion, and drug trafficking. Hostages like Lizcano became symbols of the human cost of the conflict, with many spending years — sometimes over a decade — chained or shackled in remote jungle camps as the FARC used them as bargaining chips in failed peace negotiations and prisoner exchange talks.

Lizcano's escape added to a string of high-profile hostage releases and rescues during that period, which included the dramatic 2008 military rescue of politician Ingrid Betancourt and several other hostages in an operation that dealt a significant blow to the FARC's prestige and morale. Combined with a wave of defections encouraged by government incentive programs, these developments placed increasing pressure on the FARC leadership and contributed to the group's eventual decision to enter into peace negotiations with the Colombian government in the years that followed.

For Lizcano personally, the escape marked the end of a harrowing chapter defined by uncertainty, illness, and the constant fear of never seeing his family again. His case, like those of other long-term FARC hostages, drew international attention to the plight of Colombia's kidnapping victims and underscored the human toll of one of Latin America's longest-running armed conflicts.

# Colombian Politician Escapes Rebel Captivity After Eight Years in Jungle

*Bogotá, Colombia* — A former regional legislator who vanished into Colombia's dense eastern jungles eight years ago emerged this week from captivity, walking for three days through dense underbrush before reaching a military checkpoint near the Meta department border.

The politician, whose family had long feared he was dead, was abducted in 2016 during a resurgence of violence involving dissident rebel factions who rejected the historic peace accords signed that same year. Unlike many hostages held for ransom or political leverage, his captors reportedly moved him repeatedly between remote camps, making rescue operations nearly impossible for military intelligence to track.

According to preliminary accounts from Colombian military officials, the escape occurred during a chaotic reshuffling of a dissident encampment, possibly linked to internal power struggles among rebel commanders. Taking advantage of the confusion, he slipped away at night, relying on skills and geographic knowledge accumulated over nearly a decade of forced marches through the same terrain.

"He was gaunt, sunburned, but alive," said a military spokesperson who confirmed his identity through biometric verification upon arrival at a nearby base. "His resilience after so many years is extraordinary."

## Echoes of a Famous Rescue

The dramatic escape inevitably invites comparison to the 2008 rescue of Ingrid Betancourt, the French-Colombian presidential candidate whose six-and-a-half-year captivity at the hands of FARC guerrillas captivated international attention. Betancourt's release came through **Operation Jaque**, a meticulously planned military deception in which soldiers posed as humanitarian workers to trick her captors into handing her over without firing a shot.

That operation became a symbol of both the brutality of Colombia's decades-long conflict and the ingenuity required to end it — inspiring books, films, and renewed international pressure on armed groups to release remaining hostages.

This latest case, however, unfolded differently: not through elaborate military strategy, but through opportunism and endurance. Analysts note that such self-directed escapes have become slightly more common in recent years as splintered rebel factions — no longer under unified FARC command since the 2016 peace deal — struggle to maintain the same level of control over captives that once characterized the conflict.

## A Family's Long Wait
